summary: Mobility is near normal with an MF-Index of 71, but public transport ridership remains below pre‑pandemic levels and actual fuel savings are far short of the theoretical ceiling. High‑risk sectors show limited work‑from‑home adoption, creating equity and congestion concerns that require targeted policy action.

signals.detail: The modelled ceiling of 35.7 million litres saved per week contrasts sharply with the measured 334,000 litres saved in the first week of the mandate, indicating a compliance gap of over 99% and minimal real‑world fuel savings to date.
Daily PT trips total 1.24 million (≈451 million annually), about 10% below the 2025 recovery level of 506 million, suggesting ridership is stabilising but still lagging behind pre‑pandemic demand.

Retail & Services, Logistics, and Construction sectors exhibit mobility scores of 85‑95 with WFH rates below 15%, raising the risk of congestion, higher fuel consumption and emissions that could strain urban economies.
WFH adoption is uneven: public/GLC employees enjoy 60% WFH while construction workers have only 5%, creating disparate exposure to commuting costs and environmental impacts across the workforce.

RON95 price at RM3.87 / litre provides a price signal that could encourage a shift to public transport, but the modest ridership rebound indicates that additional incentives are needed to translate price pressure into lasting modal change.

recommendation: Introduce a tiered compliance monitoring framework that ties fuel tax rebates to verified WFH adoption in high‑risk sectors, while expanding targeted PT subsidies and service frequency to lift annual ridership to 500 million by 2027. Set a concrete target of achieving at least 5 million litres of real fuel savings per week within the next six months.
